# [EP 12: Ship It]{.flow} {.title}

## One week to launch

Demo Day is **next week**: every group presents in Session XIII. The order comes out of a hat. The hat is Python.

. . .

Before you build: the mark that AI text now carries, and what AI means for your first job.

# [The Mark]{.flow} {.title}

## Could anyone tell?

- Your README carries an AI-disclosure section. Suppose you skipped it: could anyone [prove]{.highlight} that an AI wrote part of your work?
- Since August 2026, EU rules require providers to mark AI content machine-readably, and the major ones do
- The trick behind it is simple enough for three slides

## How a watermark hides in plain text

- Before each word, the model splits its vocabulary into a **green** and a **red** half, reshuffled at every step
- It then softly prefers green words. The text still reads completely normally
- By chance, a human writes about half green words. A model writes far more

## You already know the mechanism

- Session VI: the model picks a [likely]{.highlight} next token, never *the* next token
- A watermark is that choice, steered on purpose: green wins a little more often than chance
- Same next-token choice, one hidden thumb on the scale

## Who can actually detect it

- Detection is [counting]{.highlight}: one paragraph of marked text can push chance below 1 in 10 trillion
- But you need the secret key that decided which half was green
- In practice, only the provider can run the test

## What a mark proves (and does not)

- Proves: a model [processed]{.highlight} this text
- Does not prove: who did the work, or whether a human verified it
- Heavy editing can wash a mark out, and short snippets may not carry one, so an absence proves nothing

. . .

Presence without disclosure, though, looks exactly like what it is.

## Disclosure is part of the work

- The rules converged everywhere: AI cannot be an author, and its use gets disclosed
- Your README section says which tool, for what, and what you verified yourself
- That is [standard practice]{.highlight}, not a confession

# [Your Future with AI]{.flow} {.title}

## AI and your first job

- Thousands of developers: **+26%** tasks done with AI, [juniors gained most]{.highlight} [@cui_effects_2026]
- Experienced developers on their own code: **19% slower**, while *feeling* 20% faster [@becker_measuring_2025]
- Learners with AI: **50%** on a mastery quiz vs **67%** without, worst on **debugging** [@shen_how_2026]
- The fix: hints instead of finished solutions erased the harm [@bastani_generative_2025]. Part I was exactly that

## What stays valuable

- The verification boundary: usable delegation ends where your ability to **check** ends. Growing that boundary outward is your career
- [Comprehension debt]{.highlight}: code that works today but nobody understands tomorrow. The interest comes due when a reviewer asks "why does this work?"
- Your edge, deliberately kept: **explain every line before you accept it**, and code without AI sometimes

## Discussion: your future with AI

:::{.callout-note}
Three questions, five minutes, show of hands:

- Which task from the past weeks would you **never** delegate to an AI?
- What will an entry-level logistics analyst do in 2030, when AI drafts the first version of everything?
- If AI writes most junior code, where do the senior people come from?
:::

# [Definition of Done]{.flow} {.title}

## Before you call it finished

- The repo runs from a fresh clone (cloned once more into an empty folder): `uv sync`, then your script
- The README says what it does, how to run it, and carries the **AI disclosure section**
- The commit history tells the story: small steps, messages that mean something
- `git status` is clean: all committed, nothing important ignored
- I am invited, and the link is on Moodle before your demo

. . .

:::{.callout-tip}
Run the fresh-clone test **today**, not on demo morning. It always finds something.
:::

# [Wrap-up]{.flow} {.title}

## Four things to remember

- AI text carries a [watermark]{.highlight} now: fluent, normal-looking, detectable by the provider
- Your edge: [explain every line]{.highlight} before you accept it
- The fresh-clone test is the cheapest bug you will ever catch
- A demo is the thing running, the history, and the disclosure
